card.hook: Picture the whole red-walled Alhambra sitting on its hill with the snowy Sierra Nevada behind it, and you not having to elbow anyone for it. That's the view from across the valley, and it's a good one.
card.stand_here: Head for the Mirador de San Nicolás square and stand on the left side of the esplanade as you face the Alhambra, near the low wall rather than in the middle. Face south-east, across the Darro valley.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole Alhambra and Generalife in with the mountains behind. Then try 2x (or higher, depending on your phone) to pick out the towers and palace walls. Skip 0.5x here, because it shrinks the Alhambra and adds lots of foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red walls, then drag the slider down a touch so it's a bit darker and the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning or golden hour is best. The square fills up near sunset, so get there well before, or stand off-centre.
card.selfie_here: On the plaza at the Mirador de San Nicolás, turn your back to the Alhambra and use the front camera with the palace over your shoulder, but expect crowds. For fewer people, try the long garden terrace at Carmen de la Victoria, where trimmed trees and greenery frame you. Spots are based on visitor descriptions, so check the exact position when you arrive.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the Nasrid Palaces, so keep yours in your bag once you're in there.
card.challenge: Can you get the red walls, the Generalife gardens and the Sierra Nevada all in one frame, with not a single stranger's head in the way?
card.good_to_know: The name Alhambra comes from the Arabic for 'the red one', after the reddish rammed-earth walls. Building began in 1238 under Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, and over the centuries it grew into a small royal city. Charles V added a Renaissance palace in 1526, and today the whole site is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

card.hook: Picture a stone room that's dim and quiet, with little stars of daylight poking through the ceiling. That's El Bañuelo, a 1,000-year-old-ish bathhouse tucked beside the Darro River, and it's made for photos.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, which sits right at El Bañuelo in Granada's Albaicín quarter. Once inside, take your main shots from the doorways between rooms, facing along the line of columns and horseshoe arches.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the rooms and arches. Drop to 0.5x in the smaller chambers where you can't step back, and try zoom 2x or more (depending on your phone) for column tops and skylights.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest skylight, then slide the brightness down a little so the vault keeps its detail and the light beams stay clear.
card.best_time: Go around the middle of the day, when the skylights are brightest and beams of light cross the dim rooms. Early or late in the day usually means fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Try the small courtyard with the pool at Carrera del Darro 31, which leads into the baths. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the bathhouse behind your shoulder. It's our best pick for a selfie with the landmark behind you, though we couldn't confirm it as a favourite spot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Puente del Cadí bridge, opposite the baths, while you pose on the Darro riverbank by the baths so you're both in frame across the river.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos inside are fine without flash, and flash should be avoided to protect the stonework. Floors are uneven and some areas are dimly lit, so watch your step. Check the official site before you go for any photography rules.
card.challenge: Find the arch where the columns sit evenly on both sides of your screen, then get a shot with one star-shaped skylight glowing in the vault.
card.good_to_know: El Bañuelo is a preserved Islamic bathhouse, traditionally dated to the 11th century, though some researchers think it's 12th century or later. It was used as a bathhouse until the 16th century, then became a public laundry and later a home. It's the only restored hammam in Granada, outside the Alhambra, that the public can visit.

card.hook: Look up at Granada Cathedral and you'll spot what's missing: two 81-metre towers were planned, and nobody ever finished them. The huge pale front still looks pretty grand without them.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza de las Pasiegas, directly in front of the main west façade, and face the cathedral. It's an open pedestrian square, so there's no traffic between you and the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole façade in from the square, then try 1x for a more natural, less stretched look. Use 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the carved details on the arches and pillars.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and hold your phone upright and level so the tall lines of the façade stay straight.
card.best_time: Early in the day the square is quieter, so you get a clearer front view. Late afternoon may suit the west-facing front, but check the light when you arrive.
card.selfie_here: Head to Plaza de la Romanilla and stand on the paved ground with the cathedral filling the background and palm trees around you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the cathedral over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand facing you while you stand in the middle of Plaza de Bib-Rambla by the Fountain of the Giants, so the cathedral sits in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos are allowed inside the cathedral if you don't disturb people praying, but visitors can't go in during services. No photos at all in the Royal Chapel next door. Selfie sticks are forbidden in most Granada locations, so leave yours in your bag. During Holy Week, official stands in the square can block the view.
card.challenge: Wait for a gap in the crowd and catch one person walking across the square, so the giant façade looks properly giant.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1518 on the site of the city's main mosque and took 181 years. Diego de Siloé took over the design in 1529, and Alonso Cano reworked the main façade with Baroque touches in 1667. The result is a front shaped like a triumphal arch, with three great arched openings.

card.stand_here: Stand on the Mirador de San Miguel Alto, the high terrace beside the hermitage. Face out over the Sacromonte hillside towards the Alhambra, with the city spread out below.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the full sweep of hillside, city and Alhambra. Then try 1x for a calmer view, and 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Alhambra or a cluster of white houses.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the horizon on the top third line, then tap the Alhambra and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.

card.selfie_here: Try the esplanade of the Sacromonte Abbey, reached by walking up Calle Siete Cuestas. It's described as one of the most photographed views of the city, with the Alhambra in the frame. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the Alhambra over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Camino del Sacromonte path facing the cave fronts while you stand in front of the caves, with the Albaicín on the hill behind them; late afternoon is best, when the western sun lights up the cave fronts.
card.rules_and_safety: At the Sacromonte Abbey, photos and videos are only allowed without flash, spotlights or selfie sticks. Keep a firm grip on your phone, and don't accept rosemary offered on the street, as you may be expected to pay for it. The climb is steep, so wear sensible shoes.
card.challenge: Get the Alhambra and one whitewashed cave house in the same shot, then see if your friends can spot both.
card.good_to_know: The cave houses are thought to date from the 16th century, and no two are the same because each follows the shape of the hill. The area has long been linked with Granada's Romani community, who settled in the city after 1492. Sacromonte takes its name from the 'Lead Books' story of the late 1590s, which led to the Abbey of Sacromonte being built in the 17th century.

card.hook: Picture a small square in the Albaicín, packed with people all holding their phones up at the same hill. That hill is the Generalife, the Nasrid rulers' summer escape, sitting green beside the red Alhambra walls with mountains behind.
card.stand_here: Stand in Mirador de San Nicolás, the small square in front of the San Nicolás church. It's about 801 m north-west of the Generalife, so look south-east across the valley and you'll find it on the left of your view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the Alhambra hill, the mountains and the city in one shot. Then try zoom 2x or 5x to pick out the Generalife and its terraces. Skip zoom 0.5x for the main view, because it makes the Generalife tiny. Save it for rooftops and sky.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the Generalife on the left third, then tap it and slide a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out the red walls.
card.best_time: Go for sunset, when the light hits the red walls. The square gets very crowded, so arrive early to claim a clear spot.
card.selfie_here: For a selfie with the Generalife right behind you, go inside to the Patio de la Acequia, the long water-channel courtyard. Stand near the far end by the summer-palace pavilion so it should be behind you, then use the front camera and zoom 0.5x to fit in the pool and cypress-lined arches. Another option is the highest terrace, where you face the Albaicín and the Generalife is behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by in the open gardens around the Partal Palace to step back, while you stand so the Generalife hillside fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Flash is prohibited throughout the Generalife and attendants enforce it. Selfie sticks are banned inside the Nasrid Palaces and other indoor spaces. Outdoors it's less clear, so check with staff. Drones are prohibited. The gardens and palace need an Alhambra/Generalife ticket, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take the same view at zoom 1x, 2x and 5x while you wait for the light, then pick your favourite and see if it's the one you expected.
card.good_to_know: The Generalife was the summer palace and country estate of the Nasrid rulers of Granada. Its gardens are laid out on three long terraces, each about 35 metres wide and 250 metres long. The palace is thought to date from the end of the 13th century, probably under Muhammad II, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site with the Alhambra since 1984.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Mirador de San Nicolás, the small square in front of the San Nicolás church. It's about 801 m north-west of the Generalife, so look south-east across the valley and you'll find it on the left of your view.

card.hook: The best picture of the Royal Chapel isn't inside, because photos are banned in there. It's out on a narrow street, where the carved stone fills the view and you don't need any tricks.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Oficios, directly opposite the chapel's small Plateresque façade. Face the carved entrance and let the street frame it for you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole façade. If the street is too tight, drop to 0.5x to fit the entrance in, then try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) for the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the doorway up with the central line, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean inwards.
card.best_time: Morning is best, when the sun falls on the façade. Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light on the stone.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza de la Catedral, the square in front of the cathedral's main entrance, with the chapel's exterior behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold it a bit low so the building sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to a passer-by on Calle de los Oficios and stand in front of the chapel's façade, so the whole front fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography and video aren't allowed inside the chapel, but you can photograph the outside freely. It's still a place of worship and is sometimes closed to visitors, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take two shots from the same spot: one wide shot of the entrance in its street, and one close-up of a single carved detail. Then see if friends can match the close-up to the doorway.
card.good_to_know: The Royal Chapel of Granada was built between 1505 and 1517 in the late Gothic, Isabelline style, right beside Granada Cathedral. It was planned as the burial place of Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand, and their tomb is still here. Next door is the Lonja, a building from 1518 that was once used for banking and commerce.

card.hook: Picture a lane so narrow that the Cathedral tower sits right in the gap at the end, like it's been put there for your photo. That's the Alcaicería's north arch, and it's the shot to get.
card.stand_here: Head for the north entrance arch on Calle Alcaicería (from there, the Alcaicería is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west). Stand on the north side and face south, so the arch frames the Cathedral tower.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the arch, the lane and the tower in one frame. Try 2x to bring the tower closer, or 0.5x at the other entrance to catch more patterned detail and colourful shop fronts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, centre the arch and keep your phone level so the lane's sides stay straight, with the tower sitting in the opening.
card.best_time: Go in the morning, before about 10 am, when the shops are shut and the lanes are quiet. After about 11 am the crowds and street stalls start getting in your picture.
card.selfie_here: Stand just outside the north entrance arch on Calle Alcaicería with the lanes behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to squeeze the arch in, and keep it over your shoulder. The market's second Moorish archway at the other entrance gives you a different backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open market street, so be discreet and considerate. Ask before pointing your phone at people working in their shops.
card.challenge: Get the Cathedral tower sitting dead centre in the arch opening, with no photobombers. Take a few frames in a row and pick the cleanest.
card.good_to_know: The Alcaicería stands on the site of the old Nasrid silk bazaar, which was locked and guarded at night. That bazaar burned down in 1843, and the market was rebuilt much smaller in a Neo-Moorish style that imitates Nasrid architecture. A plan from 1787 shows up to 152 shops, so today's lanes are only a remnant of the original.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the north entrance arch on Calle Alcaicería (from there, the Alcaicería is about 1 minute on foot to the south-west). Stand on the north side and face south, so the arch frames the Cathedral tower.

card.hook: You've been wandering through the Moorish palaces, and then you turn a corner and there's a huge, plain stone block that looks like it got lost on the way to Italy. That clash is exactly why it makes such a striking photo.
card.stand_here: Stand on the open forecourt in front of the west façade, the palace's main front, and face the monumental doorway. Step back as far as the space allows so the whole front fits.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x and stay back. If the façade still won't fit, tap 0.5x. Save zoom 2x or higher for close shots of the carved medallions and the doorway (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, centre the doorway and keep your phone level instead of tilting it up, so the walls stay straight and the building doesn't lean back.
card.best_time: Go in the golden hour before sunset, when the warm light brings out the colour of the stone. If the sky looks bright, tap the stonework and drag the slider to darker so the carved details don't wash out.
card.selfie_here: Try the southern façade, the most decorated side. Stand in front of it near the ornate entrances, use the front camera and tap 0.5x so the stonework and doorways fit over your shoulder. Inside, the curved staircases of the round courtyard, with the double colonnade behind you, make a neat symmetrical selfie.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed throughout the palace, but flash may be restricted in museum spaces. Entry rules differ for the façade, the courtyard and the museums, so check the Alhambra's official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the doorway dead centre, the walls perfectly straight, and just a sliver of garden at the edge of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Work began in 1527 to designs by Pedro Machuca, who had trained in Italy, and stopped for good in 1637. The building had no roof until 1967. It's about 63 metres along each side and 17 metres high, with a surprising round courtyard inside. Today it houses the Alhambra Museum on the ground floor and the Fine Arts Museum of Granada upstairs.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the open forecourt in front of the west façade, the palace's main front, and face the monumental doorway. Step back as far as the space allows so the whole front fits.

card.hook: Twelve stone lions are holding up a fountain, and every one of them seems to be photobombing the arcade behind. This courtyard is small and perfectly symmetrical, so even your first snap will look good.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, right beside the fountain in the Court of the Lions. Face north towards the Hall of the Two Sisters, then turn around to shoot the other sides of the court.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole court and the fountain into one frame. Switch to 1x for a natural view of the arcades, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the lions and the carved details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines to keep the arcades straight, because this place is so symmetrical that a wonky line really shows.
card.best_time: Try the start or end of your entry slot, when there tend to be fewer people. Soft, even daylight is kindest to the carved stone, while strong midday sun can leave deep shadows in the arcades.
card.selfie_here: Crouch low beside the lion fountain, near the basin, and use the front camera so the colonnade rises up behind you. Try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the arcade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the north side of the courtyard facing south, while you stand at the fountain, so you're in the foreground with the whole arcade behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed inside the Nasrid Palaces, and flash is prohibited too. Watch your step, because water channels run all over the palace complex.
card.challenge: Can you get all twelve lions into one shot without a stranger's elbow in it? Wait for a gap between groups and go for it.
card.good_to_know: The Sultan Muhammad V commissioned the Court of the Lions, and it was built during his second reign, between 1362 and 1391. The name 'Lions' is a modern one, taken from the sculptures. The halls around the court are known for some of the most elaborate stalactite-like vaults (muqarnas) in the Islamic world.

card.hook: Picture a crowd lined up along a railing in the Albaicín, all pointing their phones at one glowing red fortress on the hill opposite. That's the Alcazaba, and you're about to take a better shot of it than most of them.
card.stand_here: Head to the Mirador de San Nicolás, the terrace in the Albaicín that faces the Alhambra hill, and face south-east. You'll see the whole hill head-on, with the Alcazaba and palace towers along the ridge and the Sierra Nevada behind.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole hill with the mountains behind it. Then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Alcazaba's towers and walls. Rest your phone against the railing or a wall to keep it steady, and take a few shots in case someone walks through.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the red walls, then slide the brightness a little darker so the sky stays blue and the walls don't wash out.
card.best_time: Sunset is the showstopper, because the warm light brings out the red in the walls. It also gets very busy then, so arrive early if you want room at the railing. Early morning is quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try Plaza Nueva, where the Alcazaba is in view from the cafe terraces and shops. Or walk the Paseo de los Tristes along the Darro, with the Alhambra's towers rising behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x with the towers over your shoulder, and check that the Alcazaba is actually in the frame.
card.ask_someone: At the Mirador de San Nicolás, hand your phone to a passer-by, stand with the Alhambra complex behind you, and ask them to frame you with it.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks aren't allowed in the Nasrid Palaces or other enclosed areas of the Alhambra complex. If you visit in winter, the Alcazaba battlements are very exposed, with wind chill and slippery surfaces.
card.challenge: Can you get the Alcazaba's red walls, a patch of blue sky and the snowy-looking Sierra Nevada in one shot, with the hill line sitting on the lower third of your gridlines?
card.good_to_know: The Alcazaba is the oldest surviving part of the whole Alhambra. Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar, founder of the Nasrid dynasty, built it after 1238 on the site of an earlier 11th-century fortress. The walls are mostly rammed earth, and the Torre del Homenaje stands 26 m tall.

card.hook: Here's a funny one: there's a square called Puerta Real, but the royal gate is long gone. What you get instead is the real Granada show, with cafés, shops and people crossing in every direction.
card.stand_here: Stand on Avenida de los Reyes Católicos and face south-west, looking back across the square towards the start of the avenue. Don't walk into the square and turn round, because that points you away from the view.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a natural view of the square and the avenue. Go to 0.5x to squeeze in more of the street frontages and the open space in front of you. Use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the Café Suizo building or the fountain.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the buildings, then slide the brightness control so the bright sky doesn't make the street look too dark.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people. After dark, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against a wall or railing.
card.selfie_here: Try the steps of the Fuente de las Batallas fountain in the middle of the open square. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if you can, and keep the fountain and the square behind you. A city photo caption says the Angustias basilica towers and Sierra Nevada show in the background, so check what's behind you before you shoot. The steps come from an old archive description, so they may have changed.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines, run the line of buildings along one vertical line, and keep a band of open square at the bottom. Can you get the street to lead the eye right into the picture?
card.good_to_know: The name goes back to King Philip IV's visit on 8 April 1624. In 1515 the square was decorated with the Catholic Monarchs' coat of arms. The Darro River once ran through here until it was enclosed in the 19th century, and after that Puerta Real became more popular than Elvira Street and Plaza Nueva as a meeting place.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Avenida de los Reyes Católicos and face south-west, looking back across the square towards the start of the avenue. Don't walk into the square and turn round, because that points you away from the view.

card.hook: Calle Oficios is a squeezed little street, and everyone on their way to the Cathedral and Royal Chapel seems to be squeezing through it with you. Look up above the crowd, though, and a dark stone front with ironwork, lanterns and carved windows is waiting.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Oficios, walking up from the Gran Vía end, with the Madraza on the left-hand side of the street. Turn to face the dark stone facade and let the street walls run into your picture.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to squeeze the whole facade into the narrow street, then try 1x for a less stretched look. Use 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the lanterns, ironwork and window carvings. Keep your phone upright and level so the walls don't lean.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, use the street walls as guide lines, then tap the facade and slide a little darker if the bright sky is washing out the stone.
card.best_time: Go early if you can, when there are fewer people in the street. Come back around dusk and let night mode have a go at the lanterns, resting your phone against a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Inside the Palacio de la Madraza (Calle Oficios 14), stand just in front of the barrier at the entrance to the main display room and face inwards. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and let the room's walls and dome fill the space behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Stand in front of the facade at no. 14 and ask someone to step a few metres back down Calle Oficios from the Gran Vía de Colón end, so the Madraza is right behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: You can see the facade from the public street, but inside visits need advance registration at the Madraza information point. The front may be under renovation, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find a lantern and make it the star of a close-up, with a carved Baroque window sitting right behind it.
card.good_to_know: The Madrasa began in 1349 as a college founded by the Nasrid ruler Yusuf I, and it's the only major madrasa known to have been built in al-Andalus. Most of it was pulled down between 1722 and 1729 and replaced by a Baroque town hall by José de Bada, so the street front is mainly 18th century. The 14th-century prayer room still survives inside, and the building has belonged to the University of Granada since 1976.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Oficios, walking up from the Gran Vía end, with the Madraza on the left-hand side of the street. Turn to face the dark stone facade and let the street walls run into your picture.

card.hook: The coal is long gone, but the doorway still steals the show: a tall gateway, a band of Arabic lettering and lace-like plaster carving, all under a wooden eaves.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Reyes Católicos, on the projecting stretch near number 28, and face the building's frontage. The Corral del Carbón lies to the south-east of you, so you'll see it side-on, tucked into the main shopping street.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the whole frontage. If the gateway won't fit in the street, try 0.5x. Go to 2x for the lettering band and the carved panels.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the edge of the gateway up with a vertical line so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is your best bet, when the street is likely to be quieter and the light softer.
card.selfie_here: Head inside and stand in the central courtyard next to the stone basin, with the galleries and hanging vines behind you. Use the front camera at 0.5x to fit more of the arches in. Just inside the entrance, with the carved portal arch over your shoulder, should work too.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Calle Mariana Pineda opposite or beside the façade and shoot low, while you stand in front of the doorway so the arch fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is permitted at the monument, but the visit covers only the ground floor, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Find the band of Arabic lettering and the double-arched window above the doorway, and get both in one frame without the walls leaning.
card.good_to_know: The Corral del Carbón is a 14th-century Nasrid inn and warehouse for grain and for merchants from outside the city. It's the only building of its kind from that period still standing in the Iberian Peninsula. Its name, 'Courtyard of Coal', comes from the coal that was weighed and stored on the ground floor, and it later served as a theatre courtyard and then as housing.

card.hook: You'll probably be dodging traffic and strollers to get this one, and it's worth the wait. The Gate of Elvira is a plain, strong arch that has marked the edge of the Albaicín for centuries.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza del Triunfo, on the side of the square facing the arch, and face south with the gate in front of you. You'll get the whole front of the arch framed by the buildings around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural straight-on view. If buildings or people push you in close, switch to zoom 0.5x. If you step back to the edge of the square, zoom 2x fills the frame with the gate.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the arch, then drag the brightness slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out and the stone keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go in late afternoon, when the soft golden light flatters the stonework.
card.selfie_here: In Plaza del Triunfo, stand by the arch with it directly behind you, use the front camera and try zoom 0.5x to fit more of the gate in. For a second one, walk a few steps into Calle Elvira, face up the street and keep the gate over your shoulder. No page gave an exact selfie spot, so check the framing on the ground.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the Jardines del Triunfo and shoot across the square while you stand by the arch.
card.rules_and_safety: One Granada photo guide says selfie sticks are forbidden in most locations and advises leaving yours at home, though it doesn't name this gate. Keep your phone and bag secure in crowds, because pickpockets can be quick. Holy Week processions pass under the arch and may restrict access, so check locally first.
card.challenge: Line the arch up with the central gridline, then wait for a gap in the traffic and see if you can get the square totally clear.
card.good_to_know: The gate began as part of the 11th-century Zirid walls. In the 14th century it was rebuilt as a heavily fortified gate so it could join the new Nasrid extension of the walls. Outside it there used to be a large Muslim burial ground, the Ibn Malik Cemetery, and the Royal Hospital now stands over part of it.

card.hook: Here's a fun one: the bell tower rising over this carved Renaissance doorway looks like it's been there forever, but it only finished going up again in 1989. Nobody will know unless you tell them.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the subject, out in the open forecourt (the compás) at the Monasterio de San Jerónimo, and face the church portal and façade. The middle of the monastery lies to the north-east.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the whole portal and façade. Go to 0.5x if you want the tower and the full width of the forecourt, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the carving and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the stone of the portal, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright so the carving keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light on the stone and fewer people in the forecourt. Take a few shots in case someone wanders through.
card.selfie_here: Stand in front of the main portal on Calle Rector López Argüeta so the carved reliefs above the doorway are behind you. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if it has it, and hold the phone a little low so the carving fits over your shoulder. If you've bought a ticket, the inner courtyard with its orange trees and arches is another great backdrop.
card.rules_and_safety: The cloister, church and altarpiece are ticketed, and photo rules inside can differ, especially in the church or sacristy, so check before you go in. Selfie sticks are forbidden in most places in Granada, so it's best to leave yours at home.
card.challenge: Get the tower tucked neatly into the top of the frame, then walk in close and find one carved detail nobody else will notice.
card.good_to_know: The Catholic Monarchs founded this Renaissance monastery, and the buildings in the city began in 1504, with Diego de Siloé as the main architect and sculptor. The church is said to be the first in the world consecrated to the Immaculate Conception of Mary, and the Gran Capitán, Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, is buried there. French troops pulled the original tower down in the Napoleonic era, and the rebuilt one was finished in 1989.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the subject, out in the open forecourt (the compás) at the Monasterio de San Jerónimo, and face the church portal and façade. The middle of the monastery lies to the north-east.

card.hook: The square in front of San Salvador is so small that you'll probably walk backwards trying to fit the whole church in, and then bump into a wall. Don't worry, the carved doorway is worth the squeeze.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza del Salvador, directly in front of the church's main façade (it's reached off Cuesta del Chapiz). Face the church so the carved portal is in the middle and the bell tower rises beside it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for a straight-on, natural look. If the square is too tight, switch to zoom 0.5x to fit the portal and tower together, then try 2x or more (depending on your phone) for the carved detail and the top of the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the portal up with the middle vertical line, and keep your phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: On a sunny day, early morning or later afternoon is kinder to the warm stone than the harsh midday light. Take a quick test shot first.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera in Plaza del Salvador, standing in front of the church façade so the church is your backdrop. Zoom 0.5x helps in a tight square, and a little tilt of the phone keeps the portal over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand across the square from the northeast side, facing the main portal (dated 1543), while you stand in front of the church, so the whole façade and bell tower fit behind you. Check the frame on the spot, as it can be tight.
card.rules_and_safety: Uneven cobblestones and steps can be tricky, so watch your feet while you step back for the shot. The church is a place of worship, so check the official site before you go for visiting arrangements and dress expectations.
card.challenge: Take the portal and the bell tower as two separate photos, then see which one you like better in your album.
card.good_to_know: The church was built in the 16th century on the site of the Albaicín's former main mosque, and its courtyard with horseshoe arches is a surviving part of that mosque. The portal was finished in 1543 in the Granadan Plateresque style under Diego Siloe, and the bell tower was completed around 1592. A fire in 1936 destroyed most of the building, and it was rebuilt afterwards.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza del Salvador, directly in front of the church's main façade (it's reached off Cuesta del Chapiz). Face the church so the carved portal is in the middle and the bell tower rises beside it.
